Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little never meant being unimportant, and that everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's words came back to her. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her chest tightened. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." The words came out sharper than she meant. "It's not just about showing up, Cal. It's about being someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for far too long. Maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

# How do I export my notes?

You can export a single note or all of your notes from Notewell, whether you're backing up your work or moving to a new device.

## Export a single note

1. Open the note you want to export.
2. Click the **More** menu (three dots) in the top-right corner.
3. Select **Export**, then choose **Markdown** or **PDF**.

You can also press `Ctrl+Shift+E` (or `Cmd+Shift+E` on Mac) to open the export menu directly.

## Export all your notes

1. Go to **Settings** > **Account** > **Data**.
2. Click **Export all notes**.
3. We'll email you a download link within 24 hours. The link expires after 7 days.

**Note:** Attachments larger than 50 MB are not included in bulk exports. To keep them, download them individually first.

Still stuck? Contact our support team and we'll help.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

“I hope, my dear,” said Mr. Bennet to his wife, as they were at breakfast the next morning, “that you have ordered a good dinner to-day, because I have reason to expect an addition to our family party.”

“Who do you mean, my dear? I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope *my* dinners are good enough for her. I do not believe she often sees such at home.”

A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament at the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps what is happening is that programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Regardless of whether this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of the ease of changing how a platform allocates value, combined with the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

- **Left alone:** the "first... then... finally" sequence, the blunt "Then, they die," the colloquialisms ("damndest," "a hell of a good deal"), the Amazon examples, and the 90% figure. Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of the ease of changing how a platform allocates value, combined with the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

# Postmortem: Checkout Outage on March 14

## Summary

On March 14, our checkout service was down for 47 minutes, from 14:02 to 14:49 UTC. During that time, about 18% of checkout attempts failed, affecting an estimated 2,300 customers. A small configuration change caused it, and it went unnoticed in review.

## Root Cause

The outage was caused by a configuration change to the payment gateway's connection pool. During a routine cleanup, the maximum pool size was reduced from 200 to 20 by mistake. Under normal afternoon traffic, that led to connection exhaustion. The change passed code review because the diff looked like a harmless formatting update.

## Timeline

- **14:02** — Error rates begin climbing on the checkout service.
- **14:09** — On-call engineer Dana Whitfield is paged and begins investigating.
- **14:31** — The team identifies the connection pool setting as the likely culprit.
- **14:49** — The previous configuration is restored and error rates return to normal.

## Action Items

1. **Add validation** for connection pool settings so that values below 100 require explicit approval (Owner: Marcus Lee).
2. **Improve alerting** so that checkout error rates above 5% page the on-call engineer within 2 minutes (Owner: Dana Whitfield).
3. **Update the review checklist** to flag configuration changes hidden in formatting-only diffs (Owner: Priya Nair).

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Most weeknights I don't have the energy for a real dinner. This pasta is what I make instead. It takes about 25 minutes and uses things you probably already have in the pantry.

The trick is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and a little crisp, so they add some crunch. A good squeeze of lemon brightens everything up, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

Serve with extra parmesan on top.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

A new study from researchers at the University of Halden points to a link between napping and memory. The findings, published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition, suggest that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60.

The research team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Longer naps of more than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Still, the study adds to the evidence that sleep matters for healthy aging, and it suggests the afternoon nap is worth a closer look.

Review: *The Salt Archive* by Imogen Hale

Imogen Hale's debut novel, *The Salt Archive*, is an ambitious book about memory, loss, and the stories families tell themselves. Set in a fading coastal town in Maine, it follows archivist Ada Calder as she uncovers a box of letters that rewrites her grandmother's past.

There's a lot to like here. Hale's prose is often luminous, and her descriptions of the sea show a keen eye for detail. One line stayed with me: "The tide took what it wanted and returned only what it could not use." The first half moves with a quiet, confident rhythm, and Ada is a compelling, layered protagonist.

The book has real problems, though. The second half leans too heavily on coincidence, and a late twist involving Ada's brother feels unearned. At 480 pages, it's also just too long. I caught myself skimming the middle chapters.

Still, *The Salt Archive* is a flawed but rewarding read, and Hale is a new voice worth watching. If you like atmospheric, character-driven fiction, you'll likely find plenty to enjoy, even when the story wanders off course.

Rating: 3.5 out of 5

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice was still in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her chest tightened. Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." The words came out sharper than she meant. "It's not just about showing up, Cal. It's about being someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for too long. Maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

1. Open the note you want to export.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

"Who do you mean, my dear? I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope *my* dinners are good enough for her. I do not believe she often sees such at home."

"The person of whom I speak is a gentleman and a stranger."

Mrs. Bennet's eyes sparkled. "A gentleman and a stranger! It is Mr. Bingley, I am sure. Why, Jane—you never dropped a word of this—you sly thing! Well, I am sure I shall be extremely glad to see Mr. Bingley. But—good Lord! how unlucky! there is not a bit of fish to be got to-day. Lydia, my love, ring the bell. I must speak to Hill this moment."

"It is *not* Mr. Bingley," said her husband; "it is a person whom I never saw in the whole course of my life."

This roused a general astonishment; and he had the pleasure of being eagerly questioned by his wife and five daughters at once.

After amusing himself some time with their curiosity, he thus explained:—"About a month ago I received this letter, and about a fortnight ago I answered it; for I thought it a case of some delicacy, and requiring early attention. It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases."

"Oh, my dear," cried his wife, "I cannot bear to hear that mentioned. Pray do not talk of that odious man. A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament at the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps what is happening is that programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Regardless of whether this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of the ease of changing how a platform allocates value, combined with the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

# Postmortem: Checkout Outage on March 14

## Summary

On March 14, our checkout service was down for 47 minutes, from 14:02 to 14:49 UTC. About 18% of checkout attempts failed during that time, affecting an estimated 2,300 customers. The incident shows why configuration changes need careful management: even a small one can have large consequences.

## Root Cause

A configuration change to the payment gateway's connection pool caused the outage. During a routine cleanup, the maximum pool size was accidentally reduced from 200 to 20, and normal afternoon traffic exhausted the connections. The change passed code review because the diff looked like a harmless formatting update.

## Timeline

- **14:02:** Error rates begin climbing on the checkout service.
- **14:09:** On-call engineer Dana Whitfield is paged and begins investigating.
- **14:31:** The team identifies the connection pool setting as the likely culprit.
- **14:49:** The previous configuration is restored and error rates return to normal.

## Action Items

We want to prevent a repeat of this. The action items are:

1. **Add validation** for connection pool settings so that values below 100 require explicit approval (Owner: Marcus Lee).
2. **Improve alerting** so that checkout error rates above 5% page the on-call engineer within 2 minutes (Owner: Dana Whitfield).
3. **Update the review checklist** to flag configuration changes hidden in formatting-only diffs (Owner: Priya Nair).

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Cooking something nourishing on a weeknight can feel like an uphill battle. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta takes 25 minutes and uses pantry staples you probably already have on hand. It works for a busy parent, a hungry student, or anyone who likes good food.

Toast the chickpeas until they're golden and slightly crisp, and they give the dish its texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

It's a wholesome meal that tastes good and impresses people.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

Researchers at the University of Halden have found that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60. The findings were published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition.

The team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps longer than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Review: *The Salt Archive* by Imogen Hale

Imogen Hale's debut novel, *The Salt Archive*, is a sweeping, ambitious book about memory, loss, and the stories families tell themselves. It's set in a fading coastal town in Maine, where archivist Ada Calder finds a box of letters that rewrites her grandmother's past.

There is a lot to admire here. Hale's prose is often luminous, and her descriptions of the sea show a keen eye for detail. One line stayed with me: "The tide took what it wanted and returned only what it could not use." The first half moves with a quiet, confident rhythm, and Ada is a compelling, layered protagonist.

But the second half leans too heavily on coincidence, and a late twist involving Ada's brother feels unearned. At 480 pages the book is also simply too long; I found myself skimming the middle chapters.

*The Salt Archive* is a flawed but rewarding read from a talented new voice. Readers who like atmospheric, character-driven fiction will find a lot to love, even if the book sometimes loses its way.

Rating: 3.5 out of 5

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. All three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice kept going in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." It came out sharper than she meant. "Showing up isn't the whole of it, Cal. She needs someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for far too long. Maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

# How do I export my notes?

You can export your notes to back up your work or to move to a new device.

## Export a single note

1. Open the note you want to export.
2. Click the **More** menu (three dots) in the top-right corner.
3. Select **Export**, then choose **Markdown** or **PDF**.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

“Who do you mean, my dear? I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope *my* dinners are good enough for her. I do not believe she often sees such at home.”

This roused a general astonishment; and he had the pleasure of being eagerly questioned by his wife and five daughters at once.

A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament about how often the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps what is happening is that programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Regardless of whether this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of two things: how easy it is to change how a platform allocates value, and the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

# Postmortem: Checkout Outage on March 14

## Summary

On March 14, the checkout service was down for 47 minutes, from 14:02 to 14:49 UTC. About 18% of checkout attempts failed during that window, affecting an estimated 2,300 customers. A small configuration change caused it.

## Root Cause

A configuration change to the payment gateway's connection pool caused the outage. During a routine cleanup, the maximum pool size was accidentally reduced from 200 to 20, and normal afternoon traffic exhausted the connections. The change passed code review because the diff looked like a harmless formatting update.

## Timeline

- **14:02**: Error rates begin climbing on the checkout service.
- **14:09**: On-call engineer Dana Whitfield is paged and begins investigating.
- **14:31**: The team identifies the connection pool setting as the likely cause.
- **14:49**: The previous configuration is restored and error rates return to normal.

## Action Items

We're making three changes:

1. **Add validation** for connection pool settings so that values below 100 require explicit approval (Owner: Marcus Lee).
2. **Improve alerting** so that checkout error rates above 5% page the on-call engineer within 2 minutes (Owner: Dana Whitfield).
3. **Update the review checklist** to flag configuration changes hidden in formatting-only diffs (Owner: Priya Nair).

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Cooking something nourishing on a weeknight can feel like too much work. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta takes 25 minutes and uses pantry staples you probably already have. It suits busy parents, hungry students, and anyone who likes good food, and it should earn a regular spot in your rotation.

The trick is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and slightly crisp, which gives the dish its texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

A new study from researchers at the University of Halden suggests that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60. It was published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition.

The research team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps longer than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Review: *The Salt Archive* by Imogen Hale

*The Salt Archive*, Imogen Hale's debut novel, is an ambitious book about memory, loss, and the stories families tell themselves. It's set in a fading coastal town in Maine, where archivist Ada Calder finds a box of letters that rewrites her grandmother's past.

Much of it works. Hale's prose is often luminous, and her descriptions of the sea show a keen eye for detail. One line stayed with me: "The tide took what it wanted and returned only what it could not use." The first half moves with a quiet, confident rhythm, and Ada is a compelling, layered protagonist.

The flaws are real, though. The second half leans too heavily on coincidence, and a late twist involving Ada's brother feels unearned. At 480 pages the book is also simply too long; I found myself skimming the middle chapters.

Still, it's a flawed but rewarding read from a talented new voice. Readers who like atmospheric, character-driven fiction will find plenty to love, even if the book sometimes loses its way.

Rating: 3.5 out of 5

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that a little tugboat could matter as much as any big ship. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice kept going in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." It came out sharper than she meant. "Showing up is only part of it, Cal. She needs someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for too long, she thought, and maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

You can export your notes to back up your work or to move to a new device.

1. Open the note you want to export.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

Well, I am sure I shall be extremely glad to see Mr. Bingley. But—good Lord! how unlucky! there is not a bit of fish to be got to-day. Lydia, my love, ring the bell. “It is *not* Mr. Bingley,” said her husband; “it is a person whom I never saw in the whole course of my life.”

This roused a general astonishment; and he had the pleasure of being eagerly questioned by his wife and five daughters at once.

After amusing himself some time with their curiosity, he thus explained:—“About a month ago I received this letter, and about a fortnight ago I answered it; for I thought it a case of some delicacy, and requiring early attention. It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases.”

“Oh, my dear,” cried his wife, “I cannot bear to hear that mentioned. Pray do not talk of that odious man. Go programmers, especially those new to the language, often talk about how to handle errors. The conversation tends to turn into a lament about how many times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps programmers new to Go ask, "How does one handle errors?", learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Whether or not this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of two things: how easy it is to change the way a platform allocates value, and the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

# Postmortem: Checkout Outage on March 14

## Summary

On March 14, our checkout service was down for 47 minutes, from 14:02 to 14:49 UTC. During that window, about 18% of checkout attempts failed, affecting an estimated 2,300 customers. A small configuration change caused it, and it looked harmless when it went through review.

## Root Cause

The outage was caused by a configuration change to the payment gateway's connection pool. The maximum pool size was inadvertently reduced from 200 to 20 as part of a routine cleanup, which led to connection exhaustion under normal afternoon traffic. The change passed code review because the diff appeared to be a harmless formatting update.

## Timeline

- **14:02** — Error rates begin climbing on the checkout service.
- **14:09** — On-call engineer Dana Whitfield is paged and begins investigating.
- **14:31** — The team identifies the connection pool setting as the likely culprit.
- **14:49** — The previous configuration is restored and error rates return to normal.

## Action Items

1. **Add validation** for connection pool settings so that values below 100 require explicit approval (Owner: Marcus Lee).
2. **Improve alerting** so that checkout error rates above 5% page the on-call engineer within 2 minutes (Owner: Dana Whitfield).
3. **Update the review checklist** to flag configuration changes hidden in formatting-only diffs (Owner: Priya Nair).

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Most nights I want something nourishing without a lot of fuss. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta takes about 25 minutes and runs on pantry staples you probably already have.

The chickpeas do the heavy lifting. Toast them until they're golden and slightly crisp and they give the pasta some real texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

Serve with extra parmesan on top.

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Most nights I want something nourishing without a lot of fuss. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta takes about 25 minutes and runs on pantry staples you probably already have.

The chickpeas do the heavy lifting. Toast them until they're golden and slightly crisp and they give the pasta some real texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

Serve with extra parmesan on top.
<<<END>>>

Afternoon Naps Linked to Better Memory in Older Adults, Study Suggests

Researchers at the University of Halden have found a link between napping and memory. The findings, published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition, suggest that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60.

The team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps longer than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

For now, the study shows an association, not a cause. Whether a nap itself helps memory is a question for further research.

Review: *The Salt Archive* by Imogen Hale

Imogen Hale's debut novel, *The Salt Archive*, is an ambitious book about memory, loss, and the stories families tell themselves. It's set in a fading coastal town in Maine, where archivist Ada Calder finds a box of letters that rewrites her grandmother's past.

Hale's prose is often luminous, and she writes the sea with a keen eye for detail. One line stayed with me: "The tide took what it wanted and returned only what it could not use." The first half moves with a quiet, confident rhythm, and Ada is a compelling, layered protagonist.

The second half, though, leans too heavily on coincidence, and a late twist involving Ada's brother feels unearned. At 480 pages the book is also simply too long. I found myself skimming the middle chapters.

Still, *The Salt Archive* is a flawed but rewarding read from a talented new voice. Readers who like atmospheric, character-driven fiction will find a lot to love, even if the story loses its way now and then.

Rating: 3.5 out of 5

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice echoed in her mind. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." The words came out sharper than she meant. "It's not just about showing up, Cal. It's about being someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for far too long. Maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

# How do I export my notes?

You can export a single note or all of your notes at once, whether you're backing up your work or moving to a new device.

## Export a single note

1. Open the note you want to export.
2. Click the **More** menu (three dots) in the top-right corner.
3. Select **Export**, then choose **Markdown** or **PDF**.

You can also press `Ctrl+Shift+E` (or `Cmd+Shift+E` on Mac) to open the export menu directly.

## Export all your notes

1. Go to **Settings** > **Account** > **Data**.
2. Click **Export all notes**.
3. We'll email you a download link within 24 hours. The link expires after 7 days.

**Note:** Attachments larger than 50 MB are not included in bulk exports. To keep them, download them individually first.

Still have questions? Our support team is happy to help.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

“Who do you mean, my dear? I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope *my* dinners are good enough for her. I do not believe she often sees such at home.”

“The person of whom I speak is a gentleman and a stranger.”

Mrs. Bennet’s eyes sparkled. “A gentleman and a stranger! It is Mr. Bingley, I am sure. Why, Jane—you never dropped a word of this—you sly thing! Well, I am sure I shall be extremely glad to see Mr. Bingley. But—good Lord! how unlucky! there is not a bit of fish to be got to-day. Lydia, my love, ring the bell. I must speak to Hill this moment.”

“It is *not* Mr. Bingley,” said her husband; “it is a person whom I never saw in the whole course of my life.”

This roused a general astonishment; and he had the pleasure of being eagerly questioned by his wife and five daughters at once.

After amusing himself some time with their curiosity, he thus explained:—“About a month ago I received this letter, and about a fortnight ago I answered it; for I thought it a case of some delicacy, and requiring early attention. A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament at the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps what is happening is that programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Regardless of whether this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence arising from the combination of the ease of changing how a platform allocates value, combined with the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

# Postmortem: Checkout Outage on March 14

## Summary

On March 14, our checkout service was down for 47 minutes, from 14:02 to 14:49 UTC. About 18% of checkout attempts failed during that time, affecting an estimated 2,300 customers. A small configuration change caused it, and it got through review because it looked harmless.

## Root Cause

A configuration change to the payment gateway's connection pool caused the outage. During a routine cleanup, the maximum pool size was accidentally reduced from 200 to 20, and normal afternoon traffic then exhausted the connections. The change passed code review because the diff looked like a harmless formatting update.

## Timeline

- **14:02** — Error rates begin climbing on the checkout service.
- **14:09** — On-call engineer Dana Whitfield is paged and begins investigating.
- **14:31** — The team identifies the connection pool setting as the likely culprit.
- **14:49** — The previous configuration is restored and error rates return to normal.

## Action Items

We're making three changes to catch this kind of problem sooner:

1. **Add validation** for connection pool settings so that values below 100 require explicit approval (Owner: Marcus Lee).
2. **Improve alerting** so that checkout error rates above 5% page the on-call engineer within 2 minutes (Owner: Dana Whitfield).
3. **Update the review checklist** to flag configuration changes hidden in formatting-only diffs (Owner: Priya Nair).

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

Cooking something decent on a weeknight isn't always easy. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta takes about 25 minutes and uses pantry staples you probably already have.

The trick is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and a little crisp, which gives the dish some real texture. A good squeeze of lemon brightens it up, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

Serve with extra parmesan on top.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

Researchers at the University of Halden have found a link between napping and memory. The study, published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition, suggests that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60.

The team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps longer than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Still, the findings add to evidence that sleep matters for healthy aging, and the nap may deserve a closer look.

Review: *The Salt Archive* by Imogen Hale

*The Salt Archive* is Imogen Hale's debut novel, and it's an ambitious one, about memory, loss, and the stories families tell themselves. It's set in a fading coastal town in Maine, where archivist Ada Calder finds a box of letters that rewrites her grandmother's past.

I liked a lot of it. Hale's prose is often beautiful, and she writes about the sea with a sharp eye. One line stuck with me: "The tide took what it wanted and returned only what it could not use." The first half moves with a quiet, confident rhythm, and Ada is a layered, compelling protagonist.

The book has real problems, though. The second half leans too hard on coincidence, and a late twist involving Ada's brother feels unearned. At 480 pages it's also just too long. I caught myself skimming the middle chapters.

Still, I'm glad I read it. *The Salt Archive* is flawed, but it's worth your time and it marks Hale as a new writer to watch. If you like atmospheric, character-driven fiction, you'll probably enjoy it, even when it wanders.

Rating: 3.5 out of 5

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second ship heard him. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice kept circling. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

"The same," Iris said. "She asked for you."

A pause. "I can't get away until Friday."

"You never can." The words came out sharper than she meant. "Showing up isn't the whole thing, Cal. She needs someone she can count on."

He was quiet for a long moment. "I know," he said softly. "I'm trying."

She looked out at the concrete pillars, the flickering fluorescent lights, the oil stains shaped like countries she would never visit. She had been carrying this alone for a long time. Maybe she didn't have to anymore.

"Come Friday," she said. "I'll wait."

# How do I export my notes?

You can export notes one at a time or all at once, whether you're backing up your work or moving to a new device.

## Export a single note

1. Open the note you want to export.
2. Click the **More** menu (three dots) in the top-right corner.
3. Select **Export**, then choose **Markdown** or **PDF**.

You can also press `Ctrl+Shift+E` (or `Cmd+Shift+E` on Mac) to open the export menu directly.

## Export all your notes

1. Go to **Settings** > **Account** > **Data**.
2. Click **Export all notes**.
3. We'll email you a download link within 24 hours. The link expires after 7 days.

**Note:** Attachments larger than 50 MB are not included in bulk exports. To keep them, download them individually first.

If you have any other questions, reach out to our support team.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano didn't mean letting go of music. It meant admitting I'd stopped.

A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament at the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps what is happening is that programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or other such mechanism to handle errors. Therefore, the programmer thinks, when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Regardless of whether this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it is a seemingly inevitable consequence of the ease of changing how a platform allocates value, combined with the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.

# Postmortem: Checkout Outage on March 14

## Summary

On March 14, our checkout service was down for 47 minutes, from 14:02 to 14:49 UTC. During that time about 18% of checkout attempts failed, affecting an estimated 2,300 customers. A small configuration change caused all of it, which is a good reason to treat configuration changes with more care.

## Root Cause

The outage came from a configuration change to the payment gateway's connection pool. During a routine cleanup, the maximum pool size was accidentally reduced from 200 to 20, and normal afternoon traffic then exhausted the connections. The change passed code review because the diff looked like a harmless formatting update.

## Timeline

- **14:02**: Error rates begin climbing on the checkout service.
- **14:09**: On-call engineer Dana Whitfield is paged and begins investigating.
- **14:31**: The team identifies the connection pool setting as the likely culprit.
- **14:49**: The previous configuration is restored and error rates return to normal.

## Action Items

These are meant to keep this from happening again:

1. **Add validation** for connection pool settings so that values below 100 require explicit approval (Owner: Marcus Lee).
2. **Improve alerting** so that checkout error rates above 5% page the on-call engineer within 2 minutes (Owner: Dana Whitfield).
3. **Update the review checklist** to flag configuration changes hidden in formatting-only diffs (Owner: Priya Nair).

# Weeknight Lemon Garlic Chickpea Pasta

It's hard to find time to cook a nourishing meal on a busy night. This lemon garlic chickpea pasta comes together in 25 minutes and uses pantry staples you probably already have. Whether you're a busy parent, a hungry student, or just someone who likes good food, you'll likely end up making it often.

The key is toasting the chickpeas until they're golden and slightly crisp, which gives the dish its texture. A generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything, and a handful of parmesan ties it together.

## Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) short pasta, such as rigatoni
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and patted dry
- 3 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes
- Zest and juice of 1 lemon
- 1/2 cup grated parmesan, plus more for serving

## Instructions

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water, then drain.
2. While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden.
3. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
4. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest and juice, parmesan, and about 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Stir until glossy, adding more water as needed.

New Study Suggests Afternoon Naps May Boost Memory in Older Adults

A new study from researchers at the University of Halden suggests that a short afternoon nap may be associated with better memory performance in adults over 60. The findings were published in the Journal of Sleep and Cognition.

The team followed 1,240 participants for three years, tracking their sleep habits and testing their memory every six months. Participants who regularly napped for 20 to 40 minutes scored on average 8% higher on recall tests than those who did not nap. Naps longer than 90 minutes were linked to slightly lower scores.

"We were surprised by how consistent the pattern was across different groups," said lead author Dr. Elin Varga. "But this is an observational study, so we can't say that napping causes the improvement."

Experts not involved in the research urged caution. Dr. Kwame Asante, a sleep researcher at Westbrook Medical Center, noted that people who nap may differ in other ways, such as having more flexible schedules or better overall health.

Review: *The Salt Archive* by Imogen Hale

*The Salt Archive* is Imogen Hale's debut novel, an ambitious, sprawling book about memory, loss, and the stories families tell themselves. It's set in a fading coastal town in Maine, where archivist Ada Calder finds a box of letters that rewrites her grandmother's past.

There's a lot to admire. Hale's prose is often luminous, and her descriptions of the sea show a keen eye for detail. One line stayed with me: "The tide took what it wanted and returned only what it could not use." The first half moves with a quiet, confident rhythm, and Ada is a compelling, layered protagonist.

The book has flaws, though. The second half leans too heavily on coincidence, and a late twist involving Ada's brother feels unearned. At 480 pages it is also simply too long; I caught myself skimming the middle chapters.

Still, *The Salt Archive* is a flawed but rewarding read from a talented new voice. Readers who like atmospheric, character-driven fiction will find much to love, even if the book sometimes loses its way.

Rating: 3.5 out of 5

Bo the Little Tugboat

In a busy harbor full of great big ships, there lived a little tugboat named Bo.

Every morning, Bo chugged out to meet the ships. Toot, toot, toot went Bo, and he pulled them safely to the dock.

One afternoon, a thick gray fog rolled in. The big ships could not see the harbor. They could not see the dock. They could not even see each other.

"Oh no," said Bo. "The ships will bump into the rocks!"

Bo thought very hard. Then he remembered what Old Captain Mae always told him: "You don't need to be big to be brave."

So Bo did not hide. He chugged out into the fog as fast as his little engine could go. Toot... toot... toot went Bo.

The first ship heard him. Then the second. Then the third. One by one, all three ships followed Bo's toots safely into the harbor.

When the fog lifted, the sun came out, warm and bright. The sailors cheered for Bo, and Bo felt proud all the way down to his propeller.

From that day on, Bo knew that being little didn't mean being unimportant. Everyone, no matter how small, has something special to offer the world.

The End.

The hospital parking garage was nearly empty when Iris finally found her car. She sat behind the wheel without starting the engine, the keys heavy in her hand.

Her mother's voice kept going in her head. You never visit. You never call. As if Iris hadn't driven four hours every other weekend for two years.

Her chest was tight and her throat burned. She pressed her palms against her eyes until colors bloomed in the dark.

Her phone buzzed. It was her brother, Cal.

"How is she?" he asked.

I sold my piano last week.

I'd been telling myself for almost ten years that I would start playing again. It sat in the corner of the living room, mostly holding up mail and a lamp. Every time I moved, I paid two men to carry it up or down a flight of stairs, and every time I quietly promised it that this would be the apartment where I'd finally practice.

The woman who bought it came with her daughter, who is maybe seven. The girl sat down before anyone said she could and played the first few bars of something I almost recognized. Her mother apologized. I told her not to.

I thought I'd feel worse. Mostly I feel lighter, and a little embarrassed that it took me this long. Letting go of the piano wasn't letting go of music; it was admitting I'd stopped.

“Who do you mean, my dear? I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in; and I hope *my* dinners are good enough for her. I do not believe she often sees such at home.”

This roused a general astonishment; and he had the pleasure of being eagerly questioned by his wife and five daughters at once.

A common point of discussion among Go programmers, especially those new to the language, is how to handle errors. The conversation often turns into a lament over the number of times the sequence

```go
if err != nil {
    return err
}
```

shows up. We recently scanned all the open source projects we could find and discovered that this snippet occurs only once per page or two, less often than some would have you believe. Still, if the perception persists that one must type

```go
if err != nil
```

all the time, something must be wrong, and the obvious target is Go itself.

This is unfortunate, misleading, and easily corrected. Perhaps programmers new to Go ask, “How does one handle errors?”, learn this pattern, and stop there. In other languages, one might use a try-catch block or some other mechanism to handle errors. So the programmer thinks: when I would have used a try-catch in my old language, I will just type `if err != nil` in Go. Over time the Go code collects many such snippets, and the result feels clumsy.

Whether or not this explanation fits, it is clear that these Go programmers miss a fundamental point about errors: Errors are values.

Values can be programmed, and since errors are values, errors can be programmed.

Here is how platforms die: first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then, they die.

I call this enshittification, and it seems to be an inevitable result of two things together: how easy it is to change how a platform allocates value, and the nature of a "two sided market," where a platform sits between buyers and sellers, holding each hostage to the other, raking off an ever-larger share of the value that passes between them.

When a platform starts, it needs users, so it makes itself valuable to users. Think of Amazon: for many years, it operated at a loss, using its access to the capital markets to subsidize everything you bought. It sold goods below cost and shipped them below cost. It operated a clean and useful search. If you searched for a product, Amazon tried its damndest to put it at the top of the search results.

This was a hell of a good deal for Amazon's customers. Lots of us piled in, and lots of brick-and-mortar retailers withered and died, making it hard to go elsewhere. Amazon sold us ebooks and audiobooks that were permanently locked to its platform with DRM, so that every dollar we spent on media was a dollar we'd have to give up if we deleted Amazon and its apps. And Amazon sold us Prime, getting us to pre-pay for a year's worth of shipping. Prime customers start their shopping on Amazon, and 90% of the time, they don't search anywhere else.
